The question of whether the minimum wage kills jobs is a subject of genuinely conflicting research outcomes. On one side, a meta-analysis cited by the Hoover Institution found that 79.3% of studies showed higher minimum wages led to less employment, with stronger negative effects for teens and less-educated workers [d1], and the CBO projected that a $15 federal minimum wage could eliminate 1.3–3.7 million jobs [d7][d10][d11]. The standard supply-and-demand model in economics textbooks also predicts that raising the minimum wage decreases employment of minimum-wage workers by pricing the least productive out of the market [d8], and one study found that a 10% real minimum wage increase reduces job growth by 0.5 percentage points over time [d5]. On the other side, UC Berkeley researcher Michael Reich concluded that "a minimum wage increase doesn't kill jobs — it kills job vacancies, not jobs," finding that higher wages reduce turnover and improve worker retention [d3][d9], and an emerging consensus among economists holds that moderate minimum wage increases have no detectable negative impact on employment [d4]. Historical data from 43 minimum wage hikes between 1993 and 2015 showed that in 74% of cases, unemployment did not rise a year after the hike [d6]. In sum, the evidence is deeply divided: researchers and institutions disagree on whether minimum wage increases destroy jobs outright, slow job growth over time, or simply reduce vacancies without harming overall employment levels [d1][d3][d4][d5].
